analysis.one_liner: Doubles the Navy's authorized purchase of Littoral Combat Ships from ten to twenty.
analysis.headline: The House passed it by voice vote on December 15, 2010, but the Senate never took it up, and it died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites part of the 2010 defense authorization law to double the number of Littoral Combat Ships the Navy is authorized to buy, from ten to twenty, along with their combat and control systems. It also lets the Navy sign one or more contracts for the purchases and requires that the government be allowed to run a competition for an additional shipyard to build the ships. The House approved it quickly under a fast-track procedure, but the Senate referred it to its Armed Services Committee and never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: The shipyards and contractors that build Littoral Combat Ships would gain a doubled, long-term procurement commitment, and the Navy would gain a larger fleet. Under the bill's terms, the government must be permitted to hold a competition for an additional shipyard, which could open the door for another builder to win work.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the authorized Littoral Combat Ship procurement from ten ships to twenty, including any ship control and weapon systems the Navy Secretary deems necessary.
Allows the Navy to enter into one or more contracts for the ships rather than a single contract.

Requires that the government be permitted to conduct a competition for an additional shipyard to build the ship design, a step aimed at expanding the industrial base and holding down prices through competition.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who fund the ships through the Navy budget. Doubling the authorized buy roughly doubles the eventual procurement dollars committed to the program, and the Littoral Combat Ship program was a large, multi-billion-dollar Navy acquisition.

drawbacks.text: Doubling the authorized purchase from ten to twenty ships commits taxpayers to a far larger share of a program whose per-ship costs and capabilities were already the subject of congressional cost-limit language in the underlying law, without a separate review of whether the additional ships are needed.

The bill modifies the cost-limitation language in the 2010 authorization law to tie cost caps to contracts generally rather than to a specific procurement competition, which could weaken the mechanism Congress had used to hold down contractor costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's clearest gain goes to the shipbuilding industry, which would receive a doubled procurement authorization. For taxpayers, the cost is a much larger multi-billion-dollar commitment to a ship program; the bill's one offsetting feature is a requirement that an additional shipyard be allowed to compete, which could inject price pressure. On balance, this is a procurement-expansion bill whose benefits flow mainly to defense contractors, with any savings for the public dependent on competition that the bill permits but does not guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote under a fast-track rule, but the Senate sent it to its Armed Services Committee, which never acted before the Congress ended, so no Senate vote ever happened.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 2, 2010, and referred to the House Armed Services Committee and its Seapower subcommittee.

On December 15, 2010, the House passed the bill as amended by voice vote under suspension of the rules, a fast-track procedure reserved for noncontroversial bills that bypasses a formal recorded vote.
The Senate received the bill on December 16 and referred it to the Senate Armed Services Committee on December 22, 2010.
No further Senate action occurred before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the bill died in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers came out modestly ahead, since a doubled ship-buying authorization was never enacted and no additional procurement commitment was made. Navy shipbuilders, the bill's main beneficiary, gained nothing from its death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, who avoided a doubled ship buy

for.name: Rep. Gene Taylor
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-MS) and chair of the House Armed Services Seapower and Expeditionary Forces Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and moved to suspend the rules and pass it as amended on December 15, 2010.

sides.party_line_note: The House passed the bill by voice vote with cosponsors from both parties (8 Democrats and 7 Republicans), and no one voted against it on record; the bill died simply because the Senate committee never acted.

industries.industry: Navy shipbuilders (Littoral Combat Ship construction teams)
industries.note: The bill would double the authorized buy from ten to twenty ships, roughly doubling the procurement dollars flowing to the contractors that build the class. Taxpayers fund the purchase, so the industry's gain is the public's cost, offset only by the bill's requirement that an additional shipyard be allowed to compete for construction.

industries.industry: Second-tier shipyards seeking Navy construction work
industries.note: The bill requires that the government be permitted to run a competition for an additional shipyard to build the ship design, which would let a new builder enter the program and add competitive price pressure that could benefit taxpayers.
